description: We are a curious team that wants to give a voice to what humanity has left behind on the Moon and Mars. Our goal is to creatively and interactively tell the stories behind these abandoned objects, combining storytelling, data, and design. If you enjoy researching, imagining, creating, or are simply fascinated by space, come join us! Every skill set brings something valuable to the team. All you need is curiosity and a willingness to learn together.
summary: The Ear of Mars is an illustrated, narrated web book for kids aged 9 to 12 about NASA's InSight lander, the explorer that listened to Mars and stayed behind in Elysium Planitia. Readers follow its mission page by page: why it was sent, what it discovered and why its data still matters. They hear real NASA recordings of Martian wind, a likely marsquake and a meteoroid impact, see real NASA photos and explore the lander part by part. A gallery adds Surveyor 3 on the Moon, Pioneer 10 beyond the planets,  Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars. Our message: what stayed behind is not forgotten, it is a clue to how we learned about other worlds.
details:
What it does

The Ear of Mars turns the story of NASA's InSight lander into a short web book in three acts: Arriving, Listening and Holding on. Each of the 10 story pages combines a watercolor illustration, a narrator text built only from NASA facts and a thought bubble where InSight "speaks". The bubbles are clearly fiction and are never presented as NASA statements. The book ends with real NASA photos, an interactive “part by part” page, a gallery of other explorers left on the Moon, Mars and beyond, and a closing message.

How it works

Kids can read on their own or choose "Start with sound": an AI narration voice reads each page while the current sentence is highlighted. Real NASA sounds play with one tap, and an info button explains how NASA made each one audible (sped up or pitch raised). On the "part by part" page, kids tap numbered points on NASA's official illustration to learn what each instrument did and jump back to its page in the story. Sources and credits are one click away on every page.

Benefits and goals

The project helps kids understand why InSight was sent, what it discovered (a molten core, 1,319 marsquakes, ice uncovered by an impact) and how its recordings keep teaching scientists, as with the 2025 finding of ancient impact remains inside Mars. Real sounds and an emotional story make science history memorable, and the gallery shows that equipment left in space is a record of discovery.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single page web app), Google Flow (Nano Banana 2) for illustrations, Google AI Studio for the narration voice, ffmpeg for audio and video editing, Google Fonts (Nunito, Playpen Sans) and Netlify for hosting. No login or registration is needed.

Use of AI

Yes, we used AI tools as support. However, the concept, the choice, the story decisions, design and the fact checking against NASA sources were done by our team.

1. Illustrations: generated with Google Flow (Nano Banana 2). Every illustration carries a visible "AI-generated" watermark, and contains no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

2. Narration voice: generated with Google AI Studio. It is labeled "AI-generated voice" in the app and in the audio file metadata.

3. Claude (Anthropic): helped with research support, drafting, translating texts, the website code and assembling the demo video. The team reviewed and edited all outputs.

4. Demo video: the illustrations and voice are AI-generated, marked with a visible on-screen label and stated in the video description and metadata.

NASA sounds and photos are original NASA material and were not altered by AI. We only edited them with standard tools: for the sounds, we cut short clips, adjusted their volume and added soft fades; for the photos, we resized and cropped some of them to fit the layout.
